trip_plan.totalNote: Two days: skin over Cascade Pass to a camp below Cache Col, then cross the col and Art's Knoll at dawn, climb the north face and ski all the way out the same evening.

days.title: Cascade Pass to camp below Cache Col
days.objective: Reach a camp on the Cache Glacier shoulder
days.note: Climb about 3.5 miles and 1,800 ft to Cascade Pass, then head south up the arm onto the gentle Cache Glacier. The December 2011 party reached a hollow about 500 ft below Cache Col at dark; a 2013 party pushed on to camp on Art's Knoll itself, and Kool-Aid Lake beyond the col is the summer option.

days.title: North face of Spider and ski out
days.objective: Climb the north-face snow line and return to the car
days.note: Cross Cache Col in the dark to reach the saddle by Art's Knoll at first light, then drop to the Middle Cascade Glacier and climb the leftmost, slightly traversing snow line over the bergschrund. The last 100 m below the summit ridge is steep and can be icy enough to turn parties back. Retrace over Cache Col, break camp…

camps_on_file.name: Kool-Aid Lake
camps_on_file.notes: About one mile and 700 ft below Cache Col on a boot path. The usual first camp south of Cascade Pass and the base for Spider, Formidable and the south side of Magic.

camps_on_file.name: Cache Col and the Cache Glacier shoulder
camps_on_file.notes: The col is the gateway to everything here. From the Cascade Pass trail a boot path climbs south along the arm and onto the mellow Cache Glacier, which is corniced at the col early in the season and can need a careful step through. Parties who leave the car in the afternoon and lose the light on the climb sometimes stop…

camps_on_file.name: Spider-Formidable Col
camps_on_file.notes: The working base camp for both Spider Mountain and Mount Formidable, and the reason to know about it is that a party climbing either peak stops here while a party walking the traverse does not. The twin notches of the col divide the two mountains, and it is reached by crossing the upper Middle Cascade Glacier almost du…

trip_plan.totalNote: Three days: hike over Cache Col to Kool-Aid Lake, climb Spider Mountain from camp, and hike out.

days.title: Hike in to Kool-Aid Lake
days.objective: Camp at Kool-Aid Lake or Spider-Formidable Col
days.note: Hike from the Cascade Pass Trailhead via Cascade Pass and Cache Col to a base camp at Kool-Aid Lake or Spider-Formidable Col, roughly 6-8 miles.

days.title: Climb Spider Mountain
days.objective: Summit via the southeast gully and east ridge
days.note: Climb Spider Mountain via the southeast gully and east ridge, about 3 hours from the col to the summit and roughly 8 hours round trip from Kool-Aid Lake. Downclimb the same buttress and gully back to the col and return to camp.

days.title: Hike out
days.objective: Return to the Cascade Pass Trailhead
days.note: Hike out over Cache Col and Cascade Pass to the trailhead.

camps_on_file.name: Spider-Formidable Col
camps_on_file.notes: The working base camp for both Spider Mountain and Mount Formidable, and the reason to know about it is that a party climbing either peak stops here while a party walking the traverse does not. The twin notches of the col divide the two mountains, and it is reached by crossing the upper Middle Cascade Glacier almost du…

camps_on_file.name: Kool-Aid Lake
camps_on_file.notes: About one mile and 700 ft below Cache Col on a boot path. The usual first camp south of Cascade Pass and the base for Spider, Formidable and the south side of Magic.

camps_on_file.name: Cache Col and the Cache Glacier shoulder
camps_on_file.notes: The col is the gateway to everything here. From the Cascade Pass trail a boot path climbs south along the arm and onto the mellow Cache Glacier, which is corniced at the col early in the season and can need a careful step through. Parties who leave the car in the afternoon and lose the light on the climb sometimes stop…

trip_plan.totalNote: A 3-day, roughly 33-mile round-trip trip: two days of approach (boat/shuttle plus a strenuous climb to a ~7,400 ft high camp below Goode), a technical Class 3-4 scramble to the 8,565 ft summit, and a long descent all the way to the trailhead on day 3. Very fit, fast parties occasionally compress this to 2 days; less aggressive parties sometimes split the hike-out into a 4th day.

days.title: Boat + hike-in to Two Mile Camp
days.objective: Reach Two Mile Camp on the Park Creek Pass Trail
days.note: Take the Lady of the Lake ferry (or Chelan Seaplanes) up Lake Chelan to Stehekin Landing, then the NPS shuttle bus 11 miles to High Bridge (not hiked). From High Bridge, follow the road/Old Wagon Trail bypass to Bridge Creek Camp, continue to Park Creek campground, then up the Park Creek Pass Trail to Two Mile Camp (~3…

days.title: Push to high basin camp below Storm King
days.objective: Establish high camp in the basin below Goode/Storm King (~7,400-7,500 ft)
days.note: Continue up the Park Creek Pass Trail about 2 miles, then leave the trail around 4,100 ft at a large washout and climb diagonally climber's-left through heather, meadows and game trails. Terrain steepens and turns rocky near 6,500 ft; cairns then mark a Class 2-3 climber's trail up to the basin below Goode at 7,400 ft,…

days.title: Summit day and full descent to trailhead
days.objective: Climb Storm King, then break camp and hike all the way out
days.note: From high camp, cross the cirque beneath the west and east towers on very loose talus, staying right of the horn-shaped-rock gully at ~8,000 ft for the correct gully. A short Class 3 scramble to a notch, a 15 ft crack (Class 4/low 5th), and a final Class 3 pitch reach the summit. Fit parties reverse the route back to c…

camps_on_file.name: Rib camp below Storm King/Goode basin
camps_on_file.notes: Flat, grassy camp on a small NE/SW-trending rib just south of Storm King, with a nearby water source. It is reached by a mostly level traverse from the basin below Goode.

camps_on_file.name: Neve Camp
camps_on_file.notes: Under two miles from the Colonial Creek trailhead on flat valley trail, this is the camp that exists to absorb a late arrival rather than to stage a climb. Parties driving over from the west side after work can sleep here and still be at Junction by early afternoon the next day. It is deep forest with no views, and the…

camps_on_file.name: Junction Camp
camps_on_file.notes: About ten miles in, this is where the trail finally gives something back after a long forest walk, with the Boston Glacier visible through a gap in the trees. It is the natural first or second night for parties heading to Mount Logan, and the standard stopping point on the way back out from a high camp. The trail to Fi…

camps_on_file.name: Skagit Queen Camp
camps_on_file.notes: Roughly thirteen miles up the valley, reached after a steep mile of climbing through silver fir, and the last creekside camp before the trail commits to the headwaters. Remains of early twentieth-century mining work sit just beyond the camp. The bridge over Thunder Creek in this stretch was rebuilt in recent years, but…

camps_on_file.name: Thunder Basin Hiker Camp
camps_on_file.notes: The staging camp for Booker, Storm King and Buckner from the west, and for parties continuing over the pass toward Stehekin. It sits in meadows and small trees with roughly a thousand feet of climbing still to reach the pass, and it is reliably buggy in warm weather. Because the pass is closed to camping, groups wantin…

camps_on_file.name: Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
camps_on_file.notes: The eastern counterpart to Thunder Basin: the last practical night before crossing Park Creek Pass from the Stehekin side, and the staging point for Buckner and Booker approached from the east. The trail above climbs through hanging meadows to the pass with good views of Goode, Buckner and Booker on the way. Coming in …

campsite_pins.name: Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail

trip_plan.totalNote: A 2-day/1-night glacier trip: a long, steep approach day to a camp at the toe of the Colonial Glacier, followed by a big combined summit-push-plus-hike-out day (~12-13 hrs).

days.title: Approach to glacier camp
days.objective: Reach camp at the toe of the Colonial Glacier
days.note: From the Pyramid Lake Trailhead, an easy 2 miles to Pyramid Lake, then the trail turns brutally steep, climbing brush and boot-track to a campsite on the flat bench at the toe of the Colonial Glacier (about 6,100 ft). Most parties treat this as a full day in itself given the relentless gain.

days.title: Summit push and hike out
days.objective: Traverse the Neve Glacier to The Needle, then descend all the way to the car
days.note: Pre-dawn start roped up across the Colonial and Neve Glaciers, traversing west past Horsemans Pack and The Horseman to The Needle's southeast ridge; a short scramble with one unavoidable low-5th-class move gains the summit (rappel recommended for the descent). Back at camp by late morning, most parties break camp immed…

trip_plan.totalNote: A remote 3-day trip (~19 mi, ~6,500 ft round-trip gain) built around a genuine off-trail bushwhack to Trapper Lake — not a car-to-car outing.

days.title: Approach via Cascade Pass to Trapper Lake camp
days.objective: Reach a basin camp near Trapper Lake
days.note: Start on the maintained Cascade Pass Trail, then continue past the pass toward Pelton Basin before dropping off-trail into the Trapper Lake basin. The final descent to the lake is an unmaintained fisherman's path that loses itself quickly and turns into a steep, brushy bushwhack, so budget extra time and daylight for r…

days.title: South Slopes summit push
days.objective: Climb Trapper Mountain (7,530 ft) via the South Slopes and return to camp
days.note: From the lake camp, work up open slopes and heather/talus benches on the mountain's south side to the summit, then reverse the same line. This is the standard non-technical line up the peak (no pitches), but expect loose rock and possible lingering snow patches depending on season.

days.title: Hike out
days.objective: Return to the Cascade River Road trailhead
days.note: Reverse the bushwhack back up out of the Trapper Lake basin to the Pelton Basin area, rejoin the Cascade Pass Trail, and hike out over the pass to the trailhead.

camps_on_file.name: Cottonwood Camp
camps_on_file.notes: The eastern gateway to the basin, at the end of what used to be the upper Stehekin Valley road. It has a privy, fire rings, picnic table and bear boxes, though the boxes are set well back from the cooking area. Access is the thing to plan around: the road washed out for the last time in 2003 and the Stehekin shuttle no…

trip_plan.totalNote: A 3-day, ~24-mile round trip with one base camp near Borealis Lake; roughly 6,900 ft of gain overall, with the middle day given to the roped glacier/snow summit push.

days.title: Thunder Creek approach to Borealis camp
days.objective: Reach a camp on the Borealis Ridge/Lake bench below the glacier
days.note: A long trail-plus-bushwhack day: hike the maintained Thunder Creek Trail to McAllister Camp, then pick up a boot path climbing the ridge toward the Borealis Glacier to a flat camp near Borealis Lake. Parties in trip reports often arrive at camp mid-afternoon, well ahead of schedule.

days.title: Summit day via Borealis Glacier and Lucky Pass
days.objective: Climb Tricouni Peak and return to camp
days.note: From camp, rope up and cross the Borealis Glacier to Lucky Pass (the Primus-Tricouni col), then climb a snow chute and rock ramps and ledges on the peak's southwest side to the summit. Round-trip from camp back to the same camp.

days.title: Hike out to trailhead
days.objective: Return to Thunder Creek Trailhead
days.note: Break camp and descend the ridge boot path back to McAllister Camp, then follow the Thunder Creek Trail out. Weather often turns on the way out, so an early start is common.

camps_on_file.name: Borealis Glacier toe / Borealis Lake high camp
camps_on_file.notes: The working base camp for both summits, on slabs and rubble near where the lower glacier has withdrawn into a lake. Ground is sloping and loose in places, so finding two flat platforms takes some hunting; camp on rock, snow or bare ground and stay well back from the water. Zone rules mean no fires, and human waste goes…

camps_on_file.name: Colonial Creek South Campground, Thunder Creek trailhead
camps_on_file.notes: The Thunder Creek trail leaves directly from the south loop, so most parties sleep here the night before rather than driving in from the west at dawn. It is a low forested car camp on Diablo Lake and carries none of the wilderness rules that apply the moment you walk past the trailhead. Book it separately from your cli…

camps_on_file.name: McAllister Hiker Camp, Thunder Creek trail
camps_on_file.notes: The last camp with any infrastructure — a pit toilet, a cook area and a food-hang setup — sitting at about mile 6.7 on an almost flat forest trail, so it is an easy first night rather than a real approach. Most parties treat it as the staging point, then start the steep work early the next morning. Because it is a desi…

camps_on_file.name: Lucky Pass bivy, Primus-Tricouni col
camps_on_file.notes: The col between the two peaks is high, exposed and windy, and it exists as an option rather than a plan — a spot to sit out weather or finish a day that ran long. Both summits are short from here, which tempts people, but hauling camp another 1,200 ft is rarely worth it against a comfortable night lower down. Whether i…

campsite_pins.name: Colonial Creek South Campground, Thunder Creek trailhead

trip_plan.totalNote: A serious 2-day backpack rather than a dayhike: ~14 miles round trip, most of it off-trail through one of the North Cascades' notoriously brushy ridge bushwhacks, with Class 3 (one or two Class 4 moves) scrambling on Berdeen Peak's East Ridge near the top.

days.title: Bushwhack up Porkbelly Ridge to high camp
days.objective: Reach a camp in the basin below Berdeen Peak's east ridge
days.note: From the end of Bacon Creek Road (~850 ft) the route leaves the last road tread almost immediately and grinds straight up Porkbelly Ridge — trip reports call it one of the brushiest ridges in the range, with no consistent boot path despite published mentions of one. Push through brush, timber, and steep duff to a camp …

days.title: Summit push and full hike out
days.objective: Tag Berdeen Peak (6,420 ft) via the East Ridge, then reverse the entire route to the car
days.note: Finish the climb to the East Ridge and scramble to the summit (mostly Class 3, with one or two Class 4 moves near the top), then reverse the ascent line all the way back down through the Berdeen Lake basin and the Porkbelly Ridge brush to Bacon Creek Road. It's a long combined summit-and-exit day, but downhill travel t…

camps_on_file.name: Berdeen Lake benches
camps_on_file.notes: The camp for Berdeen Peak and the substance of the Bacon Creek side of this zone. The documented approach starts at the Bacon Creek road end at valley-bottom elevation, scrambles up Porkbelly Ridge, crosses the east side of the peak around 6,400 ft and drops to camp above the lake — a very big first day with about 6,55…

camps_on_file.name: Bacon Creek road end and Porkbelly Ridge
camps_on_file.notes: There is no established camping on this approach and the honest answer is to start early and reach the lake basin in one push. The road leaves the highway a few miles east of Marblemount and runs up the valley to a road end around 850 ft, from which Porkbelly Ridge is climbed trackless — steep timber, deadfall and brus…

trip_plan.totalNote: Day one bushwhacks from Diablo up the Stetattle Creek side to a bivy at the toe of the glacier; day two climbs the north face couloir and descends 6,000 ft down the south side to the Gorge Creek bridge.

days.title: Stetattle Creek to the glacier toe bivy
days.objective: Bivouac at the toe of the glacier
days.note: Leave at first light, hike the Stetattle Creek trail about 2 miles, and drop 200 ft to ford the creek opposite Davis. Bushwhack and scramble the 3rd/4th-class rib, roping up for the slabby sections, through slide alder to a bivouac on flat snow at the toe of the glacier at 4,000 ft, which has running water. Expect to a…

days.title: Climb the face and descend the south side
days.objective: Climb the north face and descend to SR 20
days.note: Go up the glacier at first light, gear up at the bergschrund, and climb the lower band, the snowfield, the crux pitches and the upper couloir to the summit ridge near 6,700 ft; tag the summit if there is time. Rappel from the top of the couloir onto the southeast ridge and commit to the full 6,000 ft south-side descent…

days.title: Day 1
days.note: Drive to Diablo, hike the Sourdough Mountain Trail and ridge to a camp near Sourdough/Stetattle Ridge

days.title: Day 2
days.note: Continue the ridge traverse to Elephant Butte's summit and return. A fit, light party can also do the full round trip from Diablo in one very long day. As an approach leg into the Southern Pickets, most parties budget two to three days from Diablo to reach Elephant Butte with full overnight packs before continuing into…

camps_on_file.name: Sourdough Camp, Sourdough Creek
camps_on_file.notes: A little over four miles up from Diablo, this is the only designated camp on the lower half of the approach and it exists mainly to break a brutal climb. The Sourdough Mountain trail gains close to five thousand feet in a bit over five miles and is routinely called the hardest maintained trail in the park; the first th…

camps_on_file.name: Sourdough Mountain summit ground
camps_on_file.notes: The summit sits a little over six thousand feet directly above Diablo Lake, and parties heading out along the ridge in snow conditions have used it as a first night. It is included because the road to Diablo is west of the seasonal highway gate and therefore open all year, which makes this one of the few high camps in …

camps_on_file.name: Stetattle Ridge tarn camps
camps_on_file.notes: This is the camp for the peak. Once the climbers' line breaks out of the trees near six thousand feet the ridge runs north-west in a long open crest of heather, gravel and tarns, and parties simply pick a spot. The best-documented ascent camped beside a late-season tarn at about six and a half thousand feet and went fo…

camps_on_file.name: Improvised camp on the shoulder of Elephant Butte
camps_on_file.notes: There is no camp at the base of this peak and inventing one would be dishonest — parties sleep where the daylight runs out, on whatever flat ground the shoulder offers. From the ridge the summit itself is not technical, more a broad lump on a crest than a spire, and the standard finish takes its gentle west side at wal…

trip_plan.totalNote: A 3-day, roughly 32-mile round-trip backpack via Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River/Brush Creek corridor to a high camp, followed by a steep, off-trail class 2 scramble (about 3,600 ft of gain in roughly a mile) to the 7,133 ft summit.

days.title: Approach to Graybeal Camp
days.objective: Backpack in via Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River/Brush Creek corridor
days.note: Start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead, climb to Hannegan Pass, then drop into the Chilliwack River valley on the Chilliwack River Trail. At the Brush Creek Trail junction, turn up Brush Creek to Graybeal Camp, the closest established backcountry camp to Indian Mountain's western slopes.

days.title: Summit day: Indian Mountain
days.objective: Climb the class 2 scramble route to the 7,133 ft summit and return to camp
days.note: There is no maintained trail above Graybeal Camp — parties leave the Brush Creek Trail and climb cross-country up open slopes toward Indian Mountain's northwest side. The peak rises roughly 3,600+ ft above the valley in about a mile, so the terrain is steep heather, scree, and short loose rock steps requiring careful r…

days.title: Hike out
days.objective: Return to the Hannegan Pass Trailhead
days.note: Retrace the Brush Creek and Chilliwack River trails back up over Hannegan Pass to the trailhead. Pack is lighter with food consumed, but the climb back over Hannegan Pass at the end of a long trip makes for a full day.

camps_on_file.name: Hannegan Camp, below Hannegan Pass
camps_on_file.notes: The obvious staging camp for a party that drives up Ruth Creek late and wants the pass behind them early. Because it sits on the forest side of the divide, the paperwork is entirely different from everything down the far side — parking pass only, no Marblemount errand. Road conditions on FS 32 have been unreliable in r…

camps_on_file.name: Boundary Camp
camps_on_file.notes: Boundary sits just over Hannegan Pass at the line where Forest Service ground becomes national park, which is exactly why it trips people up: you park under a Northwest Forest Pass and then sleep under an NPS permit. With only three sites it books out on summer weekends, and a party arriving without a reservation has n…

camps_on_file.name: US Cabin Camp, Chilliwack River
camps_on_file.notes: A deep-forest valley camp rather than a climbing bivy, and its value is positional — it is roughly where a party bound for Bear Mountain or the peaks further up the drainage stops before leaving the trail. The lack of a food locker is worth planning around, because the neighbouring camps have them and it is easy to ass…

trip_plan.totalNote: A real 3-day backpack for most parties: ~24 miles round trip with roughly 10,000-12,000 ft of cumulative gain/loss, capped by a brutal 15-18 hr camp-to-camp summit day; very fit/experienced parties have compressed it to 2 days.

days.title: Bushwhack to Thornton Pass camp
days.objective: Reach a benched camp on the Thornton Ridge crest
days.note: An easy mile of trail to Thornton Creek gives way to a steep, brushy bushwhack through cliff bands and dense cedar thickets to a rocky shoulder at ~5,300 ft. Parties typically push on to flat benches on the Thornton Pass crest for camp, arriving in the evening after a long, hot day.

days.title: Long summit push via Triumph Pass and Despair Lakes
days.objective: Climb the SE Face to the summit and return to camp
days.note: A grueling camp-to-camp day: descend heather and brush toward Triumph Pass, drop to the Despair Lakes basin, then climb heathery ridge and talus to a cliff band below the SE Face, finishing with roped pitches to the summit. The return retraces the whole route, often finishing well after dark.

days.title: Hike out
days.objective: Break camp and descend to the trailhead
days.note: Pack up camp and reverse the Thornton Ridge descent and brushy creek bushwhack back to the trailhead, often in low clouds or light rain. Many parties stop to rest at the lowest Thornton Lake on the way down.

camps_on_file.name: Upper Despair Lake
camps_on_file.notes: Not a documented camp — reports use it as a rest and water stop on the long traverse to the peak, and no established sites are described there. It is the last reliable water before the cliff band below the southeast face, and worth knowing about as an emergency stopping point if a party is benighted on the traverse rat…

trip_plan.totalNote: Hike or boat in to the Thirtynine Mile Creek area and up a brushy rib to a high camp on the south ridge saddle, climb the ridge to the summit, then exit down Big Beaver Trail.

days.title: Hike in to the south ridge saddle camp
days.objective: Reach the high camp on the south ridge crest
days.note: Hike or take the water taxi in to the Thirtynine Mile Creek area on Big Beaver Trail. Leave the trail and climb the brushy forested rib to a high camp at the ~6,600 ft saddle on the south ridge crest.

days.title: Summit via the south ridge
days.objective: Climb the ridge to the summit and return to camp
days.note: Make the summit day via the south ridge, following the crest past the false summits to a short Class 3 step below the true summit.

days.title: Exit down Big Beaver Trail
days.objective: Descend the rib and hike out to Ross Lake
days.note: Exit back down the rib to Thirtynine Mile Creek and out Big Beaver Trail.

campsite_pins.name: Saddle camp below Point 6690, South Ridge

trip_plan.totalNote: Hike past Thornton Lakes to the bivy col (~5 hrs), climb the Northeast Ridge and return to the col in a day of about 13 hours, and hike out on day 3 (~4 hrs).

days.title: Hike to the bivy col
days.objective: Reach the bivy col above Thornton Lakes
days.note: Hike to the bivy col above Thornton Lakes, about 5 hours.

days.title: Climb the Northeast Ridge
days.objective: Climb the ridge round trip from the col
days.note: Climb the Northeast Ridge from the col, roughly 6.5 hours up and about as long back down, for a day of about 13 hours. Sleep again at the col.

days.title: Hike out
days.objective: Return to the Thornton Lakes Trailhead
days.note: Hike out.

camps_on_file.name: The Triumph col
camps_on_file.notes: The standard high camp, on the col northwest of the middle lake, gained by about 1,200 ft of steep talus and grass above the lakes — roughly seven and a half miles and 4,200 ft from the car. Flat ground, running water and a view straight into the Pickets. Published elevations disagree by about 150 ft, from roughly 5,75…

camps_on_file.name: Thornton Lakes camp
camps_on_file.notes: Where the maintained trail ends, about five and a half miles in, at the outlet of the lower lake. It is the easy, legal, reliable option and the one to take if you arrive late or the col is booked out — but it leaves a very long summit day, since the col is still a thousand-plus feet of steep talus and grass above you.…

camps_on_file.name: On-ridge bivy above the notch
camps_on_file.notes: Small sites on the crest a hundred to two hundred feet above the notch, one or two pitches up the Northeast Ridge. Parties use them to shorten the climbing day, at the cost of carrying a full day's water onto the ridge. Several trip reports pass through them at dawn rather than sleep there, so treat the ground as confi…

campsite_pins.name: Bivy col above middle Thornton Lake

trip_plan.totalNote: Three days and about 17 miles round trip with roughly 6,300 ft of gain: camp on Thornton Ridge, an 11-hour round trip up the west face benches and the Class 5 southeast slot, then hike out.

days.title: Thornton Lakes to the Thornton Ridge camp
days.objective: Hike to a high camp on Thornton Ridge
days.note: Take the Thornton Lakes trail (the first two miles are old road) to the overlook, drop about 500 ft to Lower Thornton Lake, cross the outlet and follow a scratch path up to the ridge. Camp on a rocky knob at 6,100 ft just south of Thornton Pass; water is from snow patches about 100 ft below.

days.title: Climb the west face route and return
days.objective: Summit Mount Triumph and rappel back to camp
days.note: Traverse past Thornton Pass under Thornton Peak's west rampart and the Great Prow, cross two stream channels to the southwest ridge, and climb heather to a talus shoulder. Angle up dicey Class 4 rock and heather benches by the Great White Slabs to a big southeast-slanting ramp, then rope up for a poorly protected Class…

days.title: Hike out to the Thornton Lakes trailhead
days.objective: Return to the trailhead
days.note: Descend to Lower Thornton Lake, regain the 500 ft to the overlook, and follow the trail out.

trip_plan.totalNote: A serious ~8-day North Cascades expedition (roughly 48-50 mi round trip, ~18,000 ft cumulative gain/loss), compressed here into 6 itinerary cards (two of which each span two consecutive trail days): 2 days of trail approach, 1 day of off-trail glacier travel to a high camp, 1 technical summit day that commonly ends in a forced bivouac, 1 rest/recovery day, and 2 days to hike out. Build in extra reserve days for weather.

days.title: Trail approach to Whatcom Pass
days.objective: Reach Whatcom Pass camp
days.note: Two consecutive trail days with full expedition loads (glacier + rock gear): Hannegan Trailhead over Hannegan Pass to an overnight at Copper Creek camp, then down the Chilliwack River Trail (cable-car crossing), up Brush Creek Trail and Tapto Creek to Whatcom Pass. The second of these two days is the longest trail day …

days.title: Cross to Crooked Thumb Glacier
days.objective: Establish high camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine
days.note: Off-trail glacier travel: traverse the Whatcom Glacier around Whatcom Peak, over Perfect Pass, up the Challenger Glacier, across Solar Pass, then rappel from West Challenger Notch down onto the Crooked Thumb Glacier to a moraine camp on its southern edge.

days.title: Summit push
days.objective: Climb Crooked Thumb Peak via the NW couloir - north ridge - headwall - south ridge
days.note: A long, technical summit day: a 40-45 degree snow couloir onto the north ridge, exposed Class 4-5 ledges around pinnacles, a Class 5.8+/A1 headwall crack, and upper west-face ledges to the south summit ridge. Parties commonly run out of daylight and are forced into a high bivouac on descent.

days.title: Descend and rest
days.objective: Get back to high camp and recover
days.note: Two rappels off a north ridge horn on doubled ropes, then a down-climb of the couloir back to the glacier and camp by early afternoon. The rest of the day is a buffer for rest, gear-sorting, and weather.

days.title: Return to Whatcom Pass
days.objective: Retrace the glacier crossing to Whatcom Pass camp
days.note: Reverse the glacier crossing: back over Solar Pass, down the Challenger Glacier, over Perfect Pass, and around Whatcom Peak to Whatcom Pass. Fog and reduced visibility are common on this glacier and call for careful GPS navigation.

days.title: Trail hike out
days.objective: Hike out to the Hannegan Trailhead
days.note: Two consecutive trail days back out: Whatcom Pass down through Tapto Creek, Brush Creek Trail, and the Chilliwack River Trail (cable-car crossing) to an overnight near Copper Creek/Boundary Camp, then a short final morning over Hannegan Pass to the trailhead.

camps_on_file.name: Crooked Thumb Glacier lateral moraine
camps_on_file.notes: Planned camp and the base for the climb itself, on the narrow lateral moraine at the southern edge of the glacier after crossing the high bench near 8,100 ft and dropping through the West Challenger notch. camps_on_file.name: Perfect Pass
camps_on_file.notes: Planned camp, and widely rated one of the finest bivy sites in the range — granite slabs, reliable running water, and the Challenger Glacier starting at the doorstep. It is the standard last camp before roping up. Open and high, so weather arrives without warning; parties have had to navigate back down to it in fog off…

camps_on_file.name: Whatcom Camp
camps_on_file.notes: Planned camp, flat dry ground near Whatcom Pass at the end of the maintained trail and the last comfortable night of the trip — reports describe it as vastly more pleasant than anything above. camps_on_file.name: Ledge at 7,800 ft on the peak's ridge
camps_on_file.notes: Emergency ledge, not a camp — a small stair-stepped shelf on the descent ridge overlooking the precipitous east face, where a party spent an unplanned full night out. No water, no shelter, cold, and highly exposed. On a peak this far in, a benightment is a realistic outcome rather than a remote one, so it is worth know…

campsite_pins.name: West Challenger Notch / Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp

trip_plan.totalNote: A 6-day, ~44-mile round trip with roughly 12,000 ft of cumulative gain — two-plus days of trail and glacier approach each way bracketing a single technical summit day; strong parties sometimes compress this to 5 days.

days.title: Approach via Hannegan Pass to the Chilliwack River
days.objective: Reach Copper Creek / Graybeal Camp
days.note: Standard access to Ghost Peak is from the Hannegan Pass trailhead; a Ross Lake alternative climbs Big Beaver Creek and Wiley Ridge instead. Day one climbs over Hannegan Pass and drops into the Chilliwack River valley on maintained trail to a forest camp.

days.title: Brush Creek Trail to Whatcom Pass
days.objective: Reach Whatcom Pass / Tapto Lakes camp
days.note: Cross the Chilliwack River (cable car) and grind up the steep, brushy Brush Creek Trail to Whatcom Pass. This is the long, sweaty day of the approach — real parties report 10+ hours of travel with full packs.

days.title: Over Whatcom and Perfect Pass to high camp
days.objective: Reach the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp below Ghost Peak
days.note: Rope up for glacier travel across the Whatcom Glacier to 6,300 ft Perfect Pass, then continue over the Challenger Glacier and Solar Pass to a moraine camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier, directly below Ghost Peak's south face. This is the technical crux of the approach with real crevasse hazard.

days.title: Summit day: Ghost Peak South Route
days.objective: Climb the south face to the south arete, then the west face, to the summit
days.note: A roped glacier approach to the base of the peak, then low-5th-class alpine rock up the south face and arete before finishing on the west face — the original 1970 line. Round trip from high camp; descend the same way with a mix of downclimbing and short rappels.

days.title: Begin the exit: back over the passes
days.objective: Return to Whatcom Pass camp
days.note: Reverse the glacier crossings — Solar Pass, Challenger Glacier, Perfect Pass, Whatcom Glacier — back down to a camp near Whatcom Pass. Long day, mostly downhill but with the reverse crevasse navigation.

days.title: Hike out to the Hannegan Pass trailhead
days.objective: Return to the car
days.note: Descend the Brush Creek Trail, re-cross the Chilliwack River, and climb back over Hannegan Pass to the trailhead — a long but straightforward trail day to close the loop.

camps_on_file.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. camps_on_file.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. camps_on_file.notes: Spectre Peak sits well down the crest south of Challenger and Poltergeist Pinnacle is a multi-pitch rock climb off the glacier, so parties working the far end of the chain sometimes take a night out on the ice rather than commit to a very long day from Perfect Pass or Challenger Arm. trip_plan.totalNote: A remote 3-day trip out of Ross Dam: roughly 48 mi round trip with one high camp near 4,300 ft in the Access Creek basin, and a long 10-12 hr summit day with real Class 3-4 scrambling near the top.

days.title: Ross Dam to Access Creek basin camp
days.objective: Reach high camp near 4,300 ft in the Access Creek headwaters
days.note: A long approach day: drop to Ross Lake and take the water taxi (or walk the lakeshore trail) to the Big Beaver trailhead, then follow the Big Beaver Trail roughly 10-11 miles past Luna Camp before leaving maintained trail to bushwhack and boulder-hop up the brushy Access Creek drainage to a high camp near 4,300-4,500 f…

days.title: Summit day via Access Col and the SE slopes
days.objective: Climb Luna Peak and return to camp
days.note: Climb the steep, loose Access Col chute, cross the open basins below Luna's south face to Luna Pass, then follow Class 2 talus up the broad southeast slopes to the false summit before crossing the narrow, exposed Class 3-4 ridge to the true summit. Round trip from camp typically runs 10-12 hours.

days.title: Hike out to Ross Dam
days.objective: Return to the trailhead
days.note: Reverse the approach: descend Access Creek back to the Big Beaver Trail, hike the ~10-11 miles out, and take the water taxi or lakeshore trail back to the Ross Dam trailhead.

camps_on_file.name: Access Creek headwaters basin
camps_on_file.notes: The open basin at the top of the Access Creek approach, roughly 1,700 ft above Luna Camp and the standard base for the peak. camps_on_file.name: Luna Camp (Big Beaver Trail)
camps_on_file.notes: The signed camp about 8 miles up the Big Beaver Trail from the boat landing, in old-growth cedar and only modestly above lake level.
